messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Psychologist
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Transportation (Bicycle): Bicycle, Female Presence: Being alone with women, Crowding/Overstimulation: Crowded spaces
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Similar Clothes: avoid wearing similar clothes, Emotion Control: I try hard to control my emotions, Suppress Anger: never allow myself to feel or express anger
  Threat: Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
  Memory: No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind., Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Distrust Others: People are not what they seem, Inadequacy: I am inadequate

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Daniel Weber was 68, a married psychologist who had spent much of his life helping other people make sense of fear, yet he now found himself arranging his own days around it. The abuse had taken place years earlier with a romantic partner who could turn suddenly humiliating and violent, and what remained of that relationship for Daniel was not a clean narrative but a series of jagged impressions. When he tries to describe it, he cannot make a clear story even to himself; it is more like a set of photographs that flash in his mind, one frame at a time, and sometimes only the raw emotional force returns without any image at all. A glimpse of a bicycle leaning against a wall, being alone with a woman in an enclosed space, or stepping into a crowded, overstimulating room can pull him straight back into that old alarm. In those moments he feels his mind tighten around the need to manage himself: he tries hard to control his emotions, never allows himself to feel or express anger, and has even started avoiding wearing clothing that resembles what he wore during the relationship, as if some accidental resemblance might expose him.  

What Daniel feels at the time of those reminders is not just discomfort but immediate danger. When he passes a bicycle on the street near his office, or finds himself in a conference room with several people talking at once, he begins watching others closely for signs that they might harm him. Crowds leave him especially unsettled, and being alone with women can make his body go rigid with suspicion, as though he is waiting for the first shift in tone or expression that will tell him he is unsafe. These moments do not simply frighten him; they also confirm what he has come to believe. He has become convinced that people are not what they seem, that the world no longer works by any rules he can trust, and that he is somehow inadequate for having missed the danger before. He was once proud of his professional composure, yet now he is ashamed of how easily he is thrown off balance, and that shame deepens his conviction that he should be able to hold himself together better than he does.  

The more he lives inside those beliefs, the more his habits harden. Because he has come to see danger everywhere, he manages himself with increasingly strict discipline, keeping his face controlled and his anger locked away, as if any visible feeling might make him vulnerable again. That same effort to suppress emotion has made the memories less orderly rather than more; when he clamps down on anger and fear, the event returns less as a narrative than as fragments, and those fragments strengthen the sense that what happened was real and still unresolved. The safer he tries to make himself by controlling what he feels, the more those photographic flashes intrude, and the more he notices the world for possible threats. He wakes during the night to check whether he is safe, because darkness feels different to him than daytime, and the night vigilance has become part of his routine. Even in his own home he scans the environment, listening for movement, and that constant checking keeps the old images active.  

Over time, Daniel’s attempts to protect himself have also narrowed where he will go and how he will move through the world. He steers around bicycles, sidesteps crowded spaces when he can, and becomes uneasy in situations where he might be alone with women, all of which makes ordinary errands and social obligations more complicated. In his work as a psychologist, these precautions are harder to hide; he has declined some meetings, felt tense in waiting rooms, and chosen routes and schedules that reduce chance encounters. Yet each avoidance also leaves him with fewer moments of feeling settled, and the less he tolerates the reminders, the more powerful they become when he cannot escape them. The fear is fed by his own vigilance, and the vigilance is fed by the fear. Daniel now finds himself exhausted by the effort of keeping his emotions contained, by the nightly checking, and by the pressure to seem calm while feeling continually on guard. What finally brought him to seek help was the realization that he was living as if danger were everywhere and himself were fundamentally unprotected, and he is now hoping that treatment might help him recover some sense of safety and a more coherent account of what happened, even if he remains afraid that without constant control he will be overwhelmed by what he has tried so hard to keep inside.
